analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering doctor, hospital, dental, and nursing care, funded by a payroll tax.
analysis.headline: Rep. John Dingell's national health insurance bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing, and died in a House subcommittee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a national health insurance system run through a new federal board, with benefits paid to doctors, dentists, hospitals, and nurses who signed agreements with state agencies. Every eligible person could pick their own doctor and hospital. It would have been financed by a payroll tax of 3% of all wages, plus separate appropriations for dental and home-nursing care. It never got past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who qualify through wage history or benefit receipt would get medical, dental, hospital, nursing, and auxiliary services as a legal right, paid in proportion to income rather than as charity, with free choice of doctor and hospital. It also would have covered needy people who did not otherwise qualify, funded through existing Medicaid and welfare grants [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services available as benefits to eligible individuals, with hospital stays covered up to 60 days per benefit year [S2][S3].

Lets every eligible person freely choose and change their physician, dentist, nurse, medical group, or hospital, and requires services be furnished without discrimination by race, creed, or color [S3].
Finances the program through appropriations equal to 3% of all wages, so people pay in proportion to income and receive benefits 'as a right and not as charity' [S3].
Extends the same-quality services to needy people who do not otherwise qualify, using existing Medicaid and Aid to Families with Dependent Children grants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and workers, through a payroll tax equal to 3% of all wages, plus general-taxpayer appropriations for dental and home-nursing services capped by formula. Private health insurers would lose their central role, since the bill treats voluntary insurers only as optional intermediaries, not gatekeepers [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: Coverage is not universal: eligibility depends on wage history ($150 in wages over specified quarters), benefit entitlement, or dependency, and needy people outside those categories are covered only if public agencies reimburse the account [S3].
The board may limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services when personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate, and hospital coverage is capped at 60 days per year [S2][S3].

Financing depends on annual appropriations, with dental and home-nursing costs capped at small percentages of total wages through 1995, so the program's scope could shrink if Congress underfunds it [S3].
Doctors and hospitals keep the right to accept or reject patients, which could leave some eligible people without a willing provider [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — guaranteed health care tied to income rather than employment or ability to pay — is very large for ordinary families, and the bill was designed to blunt the classic objections: patients keep free choice of doctor, doctors keep clinical freedom and can choose among fee-for-service, capitation, or salary payment, and administration is decentralized to states and localities. The real weaknesses are that coverage depends on work history rather than being universal, benefits can be curtailed if funds run short, and the financing caps leave Congress room to underfund the promise year by year.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its health subcommittee, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 3, 1989 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On February 6, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor action [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill, and it never received a vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and the existing employer-based insurance system, which kept their role in paying for American health care because the bill that would have replaced it never left committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the insurance status quo

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure party lines: the sole sponsor was a Democrat, and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: A national health insurance program financed by a payroll tax would largely replace private insurance as the way Americans pay for care; the bill permits voluntary insurers to act only as agents or optional service organizations, not as gatekeepers. Insurers' interest in stopping the bill ran directly against families who lacked affordable coverage.

The bill guarantees doctors free choice of practice location, lets them accept or reject patients, and lets the majority of practitioners in each area elect among fee-for-service, per-capita, or salary payment, with rates adapted to local conditions. Many physicians nonetheless opposed national health insurance on principle, fearing government control of medicine.

Hospitals would be paid their reasonable costs for covered care, a guaranteed revenue stream, but the board could set maximum rates and base payment on the least expensive multiple-bed accommodations. The bill forbids federal control over hospital personnel or operations.

Employers would bear part of a 3%-of-wages payroll tax, but most would stop paying private health insurance premiums for their workers, a trade whose net effect depends on how much they currently spend on coverage.
